lead: Cisco's professional-level SOC cert, called CyberOps Professional until February 2026. It proves you can run security operations: work playbooks, hunt with SIEM and threat intel, investigate endpoints and malware, and automate the response with SOAR, scripts and APIs. You pass the CBRCOR core exam and one concentration.
objSub: The four domains of the CBRCOR v1.2 core exam. Tick topics as you study them; progress saves on this device. The two concentration exams are in the cards below.
planSub: Set how many hours a week you can give it. The plan covers the CBRCOR core exam's four domains by weight, then saves time for practice. Budget extra time for your concentration exam after that.

v12.label: CBRCOR v1.2
v12.note: The core exam. Passing it alone earns Cisco Certified Specialist – Cybersecurity Core. Version 1.2 added AI-powered analytics and threat intelligence. On February 3, 2026, Cisco renamed CyberOps Professional to CCNP Cybersecurity; holders moved over automatically and the exam codes didn't change.
v12.onote: Topic titles from Cisco's 350-201 CBRCOR v1.2 exam topics, shortened where long.

obj: Interpret the components within a playbook
Triggers, steps, owners, tools and the outcome a playbook drives.
Determine the tools needed based on a playbook scenario
Pick the SIEM, EDR, firewall or ticketing tools a play calls for.
Apply the playbook for a common scenario
Unauthorized privilege elevation, DoS and DDoS, and website defacement.
Infer the industry for compliance standards
PCI DSS, FISMA, FedRAMP, SOC 2, SOX, GDPR, data privacy and ISO 27001.
Describe the purpose of cyber risk insurance
What it covers, what it excludes, and what insurers expect you to have in place.
Analyze the elements of a risk analysis
Asset, vulnerability and threat, combined into risk.
Apply the incident response workflow
Preparation, detection and analysis, containment, eradication, recovery and lessons learned.
Describe incident response metrics
Mean time to detect, respond and recover, and where the process can improve.
Describe types of cloud environments
Public, private, hybrid and community clouds.

obj: Recommend AI-powered data analytic techniques
Pick the analysis that answers the question, from clustering to anomaly scoring.
Describe the use of hardening machine images for deployment
Golden images built to a secure baseline.
Describe the process of evaluating the security posture of an asset
Configuration, patch level, exposure and controls.
Evaluate security controls, diagnose gaps and recommend improvements
Find what's missing and what to fix first.
Determine resources for industry standards and hardening
CIS Benchmarks, DISA STIGs, vendor guides and NIST.
Determine patching recommendations
What to patch first, and when to test or wait.
Recommend services to disable
Turn off what the role doesn't need.
Apply network segmentation
Zones, VLANs and microsegmentation to contain an attacker.
Utilize network controls for network hardening
ACLs, firewall rules, NAC and IPS.
Determine DevSecOps recommendations
Security in the pipeline: scanning, secrets, signed builds.
Describe using a threat intelligence platform (TIP) to automate intelligence
Collect, score and push indicators to your tools.
Apply AI-driven threat intelligence using tools
Use AI-assisted intel tools to enrich and prioritize.
Apply data loss and leakage concepts
Data in motion, in use and at rest.
Describe DLP detection and enforcement
Host, network, application and cloud DLP.
Recommend tuning or adapting devices and software
Adjust rules, filters and policies to cut noise and catch more.
Describe security data management concepts
Collection, normalization, retention and storage of security data.
Describe SIEM tools for security data analytics
Search, correlation, dashboards and alerting.
Recommend workflows from issue through escalation and automation
Manual steps and SOAR playbooks from alert to closure.
Apply dashboard data to communicate with stakeholders
Different views for technical staff, leaders and executives.
Analyze anomalous user and entity behavior (UEBA)
Spot unusual logins, access and data movement in SIEM data.
Determine the next action based on user behavior alerts
Verify, contain, escalate or close.
Describe network analysis tools and their limitations
Packet capture, traffic analysis and network logs.
Evaluate artifacts and streams in a packet capture file
Follow streams, carve files and spot C2 traffic.
Troubleshoot existing detection rules
Fix rules that miss or that fire on everything.
Determine tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs) from an attack
Map what the attacker did to MITRE ATT&CK.

extras.title: IOC vs IOA
rows: Hashes, bad domains and IPs: proof something already happened.
A process dumping LSASS, mass file renames: an attack in progress.
Run the sample safely to collect both kinds of indicator.

extras.title: REST codes for SOAR
rows: Bad or missing credentials or token.
Valid login, but no permission for this.
Wrong path or the object doesn't exist.
You hit the rate limit. Back off and retry later.
The other side failed; retry or escalate.

method: Techniques and Processes are 60% of CBRCOR. Start there: SIEM, hunting, malware analysis and investigations.
Work investigations in legal labs: TryHackMe SOC rooms, Blue Team Labs, or a home SIEM fed by your own VMs.
Write small Python and Bash scripts that call a public, free API and handle 401, 404 and 429 responses.
Flashcards for IR phases, IOC vs IOA, REST codes, data formats and compliance standards.
Choose CBRFIR if you like forensics and incident response, CBRTHD if you like hunting. Budget time for it after the core.
tips: Many questions ask what to do next in an incident. Find the IR phase you're in and pick the step that fits.
Collect and preserve before you clean up. Wiping a box too early destroys what you need.
Short Python and JSON snippets show up often. Trace them line by line.
Cisco exams don't let you return to a question once you move on.

quiz.q: An alert shows a standard user account was just added to Domain Admins outside any change window. Per the IR workflow, what comes FIRST?
o: Validate the alert and scope it: who made the change, from where, and what else that account touched
Right. Detection and analysis come before containment. Confirm it's real and how far it goes.
Reimage every domain controller
That's eradication before you even know what happened, and it destroys evidence.
Close the alert as a likely admin mistake
An unapproved jump to Domain Admins is a classic sign of compromise.
Write the lessons-learned report
That's the last phase, after the incident is handled.

quiz.q: A company stores and processes credit card payments. Which standard applies MOST directly?
o: PCI DSS
Right. PCI DSS governs anyone who stores, processes or transmits card data.
FedRAMP
FedRAMP covers cloud services used by US federal agencies.
SOX
SOX is about financial reporting controls for public companies.
GDPR
GDPR protects personal data of people in the EU; it isn't card-specific.

quiz.q: Which metric shows how long it takes, on average, from an attack starting until the SOC notices it?
o: Mean time to detect (MTTD)
Right. MTTD measures the gap between compromise and detection.
Mean time to respond (MTTR)
MTTR measures from detection to containment or resolution.
Mean time between failures
That's a reliability metric for hardware.
Recovery point objective
RPO is how much data loss is acceptable in a disaster.

quiz.q: A detection rule fires 4,000 times a day, almost all from a known backup server's normal behavior. What should you do?
o: Tune the rule to exclude that server's known-good behavior, and document the exception
Right. Tuning cuts noise so real alerts aren't buried, while keeping coverage everywhere else.
Delete the rule
You'd lose detection on every other host.
Leave it as is so nothing is missed
Analysts will start ignoring it, which is how real attacks get missed.
Lower its severity to informational
The noise is still there, just hidden.

quiz.q: A user who normally logs in from Norfolk during the day logs in at 3 a.m. from another country, then downloads 40 GB from a file share. Which capability is built to flag this?
o: UEBA (user and entity behavior analytics)
Right. UEBA learns each user's normal pattern and flags big departures like this one.
A signature-based IDS
Signatures match known attack patterns, not a user acting unlike themselves.
A vulnerability scanner
Scanners find weaknesses, not suspicious behavior.
DHCP logs
They show address leases, not behavior.

quiz.q: In a packet capture, a workstation sends a small HTTPS request to the same rare domain every 60 seconds, all night. What does this MOST likely show?
o: Command-and-control beaconing
Right. Regular, small check-ins to an unusual domain are a classic C2 beacon.
Normal Windows updates
Updates come in bursts from Microsoft domains, not a steady beat to a rare one.
A DNS outage
DNS outages cause failed lookups, not steady HTTPS sessions.
A user browsing the web
Nobody browses one rare site every 60 seconds all night.

quiz.q: An attacker used stolen credentials, then ran PowerShell to dump LSASS memory. Where do you record these as TTPs?
o: Map them to MITRE ATT&CK techniques (Valid Accounts, OS Credential Dumping)
Right. ATT&CK gives a shared language for what the attacker did.
CVSS
CVSS scores how severe a vulnerability is, not attacker behavior.
The NIST CSF tiers
CSF tiers rate how mature a program is.
A FIPS 199 category
FIPS 199 sets a system's impact level.

quiz.q: You have a suspicious attachment. What is the safest FIRST analysis step?
o: Hash it and check threat intel, then detonate it in an isolated sandbox
Right. Known hashes save time, and a sandbox lets you watch it safely.
Open it on your workstation to see what happens
That risks infecting your own machine and the network.
Email it to coworkers for a second opinion
That spreads the malware.
Delete it right away
You lose the chance to learn what it does and find other victims.

quiz.q: Which is an indicator of ATTACK (IOA) rather than an indicator of compromise (IOC)?
o: A process is encrypting hundreds of files per minute right now
Right. IOAs describe behavior in progress, so you can act before it's done.
A known-bad file hash found on disk
A hash is evidence of something already present: an IOC.
A domain on a threat intel blocklist
That's a known indicator: an IOC.
An IP address from last month's report
That's historical evidence: an IOC.

quiz.q: Two vulnerabilities: CVSS 9.8 on an internal test box with no data, and CVSS 7.5 on an internet-facing server that's being exploited in the wild. Which do you fix first?
o: The 7.5 on the internet-facing, actively exploited server
Right. Exposure, active exploitation and asset value can outweigh the raw CVSS number.
The 9.8, because the higher score always wins
CVSS is one input. Context decides the real risk.
Neither until the next patch cycle
Active exploitation on an exposed server can't wait.
Whichever is faster to patch
Ease matters, but risk comes first.

quiz.q: Data from a database may have leaked. Which source shows WHO ran large queries against it?
o: Database audit logs
Right. Audit logs record which account ran which queries and when.
The building's door badge logs
They show who entered a room, not who queried a database.
The DHCP server
It hands out addresses; it doesn't log queries.
The printer queue
Unrelated to database access.

quiz.q: Your SOAR playbook calls a threat intel API and gets HTTP 429. What should the playbook do?
o: Wait and retry with backoff, within the API's rate limit
Right. 429 means too many requests. Slow down and try again later.
Treat the indicator as clean
An error isn't a verdict. That would hide real threats.
Resend the request in a tight loop
That makes the rate-limit problem worse.
Get a new API key every time
That breaks the provider's terms and doesn't fix the design.

quiz.q: What does this script print for an alert with severity 7?
o: open ticket
Right. 7 isn't at least 8, but it is at least 5, so the elif branch runs.
page on-call
That needs severity 8 or higher.
log only
That's only for severities below 5.
An error, because dict keys need single quotes
Python accepts double-quoted keys.

quiz.q: Which format is this data in?
o: XML
Right. Tagged elements with opening and closing tags are XML.
JSON
JSON uses braces, keys and values, not tags.
CSV
CSV is comma-separated rows.
YAML
YAML uses indentation and key: value pairs.

pbqs.title: Pick the IR phase and next step
pbqs.scenario: You're the on-shift analyst. For each event, pick the incident response phase you're in and the BEST next step. Some options aren't used.

rows.req: EDR alert: possible ransomware behavior on one laptop; not confirmed yet
rows.why: First confirm it's real and see how far it reaches.

rows.req: Confirmed: the laptop is encrypting a file share right now
rows.why: Stop the spread first: isolate the host from the network.

rows.req: Host isolated; persistence found in a scheduled task
rows.why: Eradicate: remove the malware and its persistence.

rows.req: Clean image applied; user needs the laptop back
rows.why: Recover: restore service and watch closely for reinfection.
Lessons learned: improve detections and update the playbook.

pbqs.title: What does the evidence show?
pbqs.scenario: Six pieces of evidence from one investigation. Pick what each shows. Each answer is used once; two options are distractors.

before: Cisco's associate SOC cert, the natural step before
Vendor-neutral analyst skills, on the DoD 8140 matrix
The DoD 8140 cert most people start with
next: The senior cert for security leaders
hereNote: Cisco's professional SOC and incident response cert
mapSub: CCNP Cybersecurity is the professional step for SOC analysts after CCNA Cybersecurity and CySA+. Tap any cert to jump to it.

keep.text: Renew with 80 CE credits, or by passing one core exam, two concentration exams, or one concentration exam plus 40 CE credits. Passing a CCIE lab also works.
keep.after: Recertifying CCNP also renews the associate and specialist certs under it.

keep.text: CCNP Cybersecurity isn't on the DoD 8140 matrix (V3.0). For the Cyber Defense Analyst (511) and Incident Responder (531) roles, CCNA Cybersecurity and CySA+ are listed.
keep.after: For a coded billet, get one of those first. CCNP Cybersecurity adds professional depth.

keep.text: Practice on your own lab, legal training platforms, or systems you have written permission to investigate. Handle real incident data only as your command's procedures allow.
